title: An audience of stellar flashbulbs
caption: The globular cluster Messier 107, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: M 107 · constellation Ophiuchus · about 20000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble's view of Messier 107 resembles a stadium with the lights down before a performance, twinkling only with camera flashes from the crowd. Unlike flashbulbs, though, these stars are no fleeting phenomenon: they have been shining for many billions of years.

The Milky Way's disc is ringed by more than 150 globular clusters, Messier 107 among them. Each of these spherical groups contains hundreds of thousands of extremely old stars, making them some of the oldest objects in our galaxy. How they formed, and what part they played in the evolution of galaxies, is still somewhat unclear, which is why astronomers keep studying them.

By globular standards, this cluster is fairly loose. Set beside others like Messier 53 or Messier 54, its stars are packed less tightly, so its members stand out more individually, like separate fans in the stands.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.42 x 3.49 arcminutes) and distance (20000 light years), the frame spans roughly 20 × 20 light-years. Its light set out about 20,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from the Wide Field Camera of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view separates stars that would blur together through a small telescope.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: About 20 000 light-years from the Solar System, Messier 107 lies in Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer. Pierre Méchain first noted it in 1782 and William Herschel recorded it independently a year later; much later, the Canadian astronomer Helen Sawyer Hogg added it to Messier's catalogue. The image covers about 3.4 by 3.4 arcminutes.
alt: A loosely packed crowd of stars in the globular cluster Messier 107.
